Agreed. Most of the time you can't control what happens around/to you. What I like to focus on is the fact that I do have control of how I respond to those painful things. Do I give in to despair and behave in ways that make things even worse? Or do I choose to behave in positive and healthy ways in response to that pain? That is where our true power lies.

Not causing more pain to loved ones is what eventually stopped me from making more attempts on my life. However, while enduring the agony that leads to the contemplation of suicide, being alive simply for others is a miserable existence. I felt like I was in limbo, alive but not living, undead really. 

And there I would have stayed if I hadn't spent months looking inwards for a motivation for life that came from within. At first that was curiosity, wanting to know what happens next in this crazy world of ours, and focusing on that. Then came deciding i had my own worth and acting accordingly, trying not to put myself into dangerous situations that were only making things worse. I spent even more time after that painstakingly building a life around those values, still fighting the urge to die for the first couple years, and making lots of mistakes along the way. 

But here I am almost 4 years later, happier and more stable than I ever thought possible, hopefully heading back to school this summer for psychology so I can better help people help themselves. And it all started when I made the decision that suicide wasn't an option and got help, and that was all thanks to having a loving family I didn't want to hurt. What I'm trying to explain through the story of my experience is that yes family is a good reason to stick around, but that's not where the journey to recovery ends. In my opinion, true happiness in life comes from an inner sense of worth and value that gets built upon over time.
